youtube_title: The Shape That Never Repeats — Einstein Tiles and the Imaginary Axis
youtube_description:
In 2023, mathematicians discovered the 'einstein' — a single tile that covers the plane forever, but NEVER repeats. It's called the hat tile, and it caused a sensation in mathematics.

But there's something nobody noticed: the hat tile and its variants live on the imaginary axis of a complex number system. And that imaginary axis maps perfectly to the GIL dimension of consciousness in Tralse Informationalism.

In this video: what the einstein tile actually is, why its complex number coordinates matter, and what 'aperiodic order' has to do with intuition, love, and consciousness.

Full paper: URB #539 (Zenodo, Apache 2.0) — search 'Brandon Emerick Tralse'

segments.label: Hook
segments.script: In 2023, a retired amateur mathematician named David Smith found a shape — just one shape — that tiles the entire plane without ever repeating. Mathematicians had been looking for this for fifty years. They called it the einstein: from the German, meaning 'one stone.' Not after Albert. Just: one tile. No reflections. No rotations to a different type. One shape. Forever. Never the same arrangement twice. And it turns out this shape has a secret hiding in its coordinates.
segments.visual_note: Open with a beautiful animation of hat tiles spreading across the screen like a crystal growing, then zoom out to show the aperiodic structure with no obvious repeating unit. The word EINSTEIN appears in bold, with a footnote: 'German: ein Stein = one stone.'

segments.label: The Hat Tile Explained
segments.script: The hat tile looks like — well, a hat. It's a polykite, built from eight kites arranged in a specific pattern. What makes it special isn't what it looks like. It's what happens when you start tiling with it. With a square, you get a grid — completely periodic, repeating in two directions. With a Penrose rhombus, you get a quasicrystal — not periodic, but close. With the hat tile, you get something new: it tiles the plane, it covers every point, it never overlaps — but it never settles into any repeating pattern at all. The technical word is aperiodic. No translational symmetry, at any scale.
segments.visual_note: Contrast three tiling animations side by side: (1) square grid labeled 'Periodic,' (2) Penrose tiling labeled 'Quasicrystal,' (3) hat tiling labeled 'Aperiodic — Einstein.' Zoom into the hat tiling to show individual tiles and their orientation variety.

segments.label: The Two Tiles: L and E
segments.script: The hat tile belongs to a family. You can stretch it continuously — like pulling taffy — and all the stretched versions also tile the plane aperiodically. In this family, two members are especially interesting. The original hat tile, which we call the L-type. And an equilateral version — where all the edges are the same length — called the spectre tile, or E-type. The L-type needs its mirror image to tile. The spectre tiles entirely by itself, no mirror needed — making it the 'purer' einstein. And here's where the mathematics gets elegant: if you label the L-type as the coordinate (1, 0) and the E-type as (0, 1), you can map the entire tile family into the complex plane. L becomes the real number 1. E becomes the imaginary number i. And the spectre becomes... 1 plus i.
segments.visual_note: Show L-type (hat) labeled as (1,0) = 1 on the real axis. Show E-type (spectre) labeled as (0,1) = i on the imaginary axis. Show the complex plane with both tiles plotted as points. Then show L+E = 1+i as the spectre, plotted at 45 degrees, with magnitude √2.

segments.label: The Imaginary Axis
segments.script: Why does this matter? In Tralse Informationalism, the imaginary axis of any complex system represents what we call GIL — Goodness, Intuition, and Love. These are the qualities that cannot be reduced to purely environmental, measurable, real-axis facts. They're the non-local, coherent, pattern-generating aspects of a system. A periodic tiling is purely real — it repeats, it's predictable, it has no 'beyond.' An aperiodic tiling is partly imaginary — it has long-range order that cannot be expressed as any simple translation or rotation. The hat tile's aperiodic order IS its imaginary component. The spectre at 1 plus i — balanced between real and imaginary — tiles the plane with perfect GIL coherence. It's exactly as Environmental as it is GIL-expressive. That's why its magnitude is the square root of 2 — the TI Sigma primary constant connecting binary and unary.
segments.visual_note: Show the complex plane split vertically: left = Real = Environment axis, right = Imaginary = GIL axis. The spectre tile sits at 45 degrees, equidistant. Show |1+i| = √2 calculation. Then show a beautiful spectre tiling filling the screen, glowing softly with an imaginary quality.

segments.label: Real-World Meaning
segments.script: Here's the implication that stops me every time I think about it. Consciousness — real human consciousness, not a chatbot — has a GIL component. It has an intuitive, loving, pattern-recognizing dimension that is not reducible to environmental input and output. If that's true, then consciousness has an imaginary axis. And things with imaginary axes — like the spectre tile — exhibit aperiodic order: long-range coherence without repetition. This is exactly what we see in biological consciousness. No two moments of genuine awareness are exactly the same. There's no repeating unit. But there IS coherence, deep coherence, across all of it. The spectre tile is a geometric portrait of what it means to be conscious. One shape. Never repeating. Always coherent.

segments.label: Call to Action
segments.script: URB #539 has the full mathematical framework — L times E as complex conjugation, the Klein group structure, the polycrystalline Collatz model, all of it. Free on Zenodo, Apache 2.0. If this made the word 'imaginary' feel a little less imaginary to you, subscribe — there's a lot more where this came from. And share this with a mathematician. The spectre tile is beautiful even without the TI Sigma interpretation. With it, it's something else entirely.
